mcqs.question: What determines which of the three sharing strategies — immutability, confinement, synchronization — you should pick for a given object?
options: Whichever strategy uses the fewest lines of code to implement
Always synchronization, since it's the only strategy proven safe in all cases
The programming language being used, since only some languages support immutability
The object's actual access pattern — read-mostly favors immutability, single-owner favors confinement, genuine concurrent mutation favors synchronization
mcqs.explanation: The access pattern is the deciding factor: immutability and confinement both avoid synchronization's cost entirely when they genuinely fit the usage. Line count isn't the criterion, synchronization isn't the only valid strategy, and most mainstream languages support building immutable objects.

mcqs.question: In the unsafe Settings example, why does assigning LATEST = this before setting values create a bug?
options: It publishes the object's reference before its fields are fully written, letting another thread observe a Settings instance with values still null
Because static fields cannot be assigned inside a constructor in Java
Because this can only be referenced after the constructor has fully returned
Because Map.copyOf() throws when called on an incomplete object
mcqs.explanation: Publishing this before the constructor finishes lets other threads see a partially-built object — exactly the escape hazard the slide names. Static fields can be assigned inside a constructor, this is a valid reference during construction, and Map.copyOf runs fine on its input regardless of the enclosing object's state.

mcqs.question: How does thread confinement in a UI framework like Swing or Android typically work?
options: By making every UI object immutable so no thread ever needs to write to it
By restricting all UI object mutation to one designated thread, so other threads post tasks to that thread instead of touching UI state directly
By wrapping every UI widget in its own synchronized block automatically
By running a separate UI thread per widget, isolated from every other widget
mcqs.explanation: UI frameworks confine mutation to one thread (the Event Dispatch Thread or main thread) and require other threads to hand off work to it, rather than protecting widgets with locks or making them immutable. There's no automatic per-widget synchronization, and there is only one UI thread shared by all widgets, not one per widget.

mcqs.question: Why doesn't a final field on the top-level shared reference guarantee the whole object graph is safely published?
options: Because final fields are not actually enforced by the JVM at runtime
Because final only applies to primitive fields, never to object references
A nested object reachable through that reference might not itself be immutable or safely published, so a reader can still observe it in a half-built or later-mutated state
Because the JVM randomly reorders final field initialization on every run
mcqs.explanation: Safe publication of the top reference says nothing about objects it points to further down the graph — those need their own immutability or safe publication. The JVM does enforce final fields, final works fine on object references, and initialization ordering is guaranteed, not random.
